🕷️ Introduction: what a web crawler does and why it is hard

Hinglish samajh: Web crawler ek program hai jo web pages par jaata hai, unka content jama karta hai aur unke links follow karke naye pages dhundta hai. Sabse mashhoor use search engine indexing hai (jaise Googlebot). Doosre use: web archiving, web mining aur web monitoring. Ek achhe crawler ke chaar gun: scalability (arabon pages), robustness (kharab HTML aur crashes), politeness (kisi website par bahut zyada requests nahi) aur extensibility (naye content type aasani se jodna).

A web crawler (also called a spider or a robot) is a program that visits web pages, collects their content (pages, images, videos) and follows the links on each page to find more pages. It starts from a few known addresses and keeps discovering new ones, a bit like exploring a city by walking down every street you see. In this chapter we design a crawler for the most famous use: search engine indexing, where a crawler such as Googlebot collects pages so that a search engine can search them.

Crawlers have other uses too. Web archiving keeps copies of web data for the future (for example, the US Library of Congress). Web mining extracts knowledge from web data (for example, financial analysis from shareholder reports). Web monitoring detects copyright or trademark violations.

A good crawler has four qualities, and these are the design challenges. Scalability: the web has billions of pages, so crawling must be parallel. Robustness: the web is messy, with broken HTML, unresponsive servers, crashes and even malicious links, and the crawler must survive all of them. Politeness: the crawler must not flood any single website with requests. Extensibility: it should be easy to add support for new content types (for example images) with little change.

Uses of a web crawler

UsePurposeExample
Search engine indexingCollect pages to build a searchable indexGooglebot
Web archivingPreserve web data for the futureUS Library of Congress
Web miningExtract knowledge from web dataFinancial analysis of shareholder reports
Web monitoringDetect copyright or trademark violationsBrand protection tools

✨ Features

  • Visits pages and follows their links to discover more.
  • Used for search indexing, archiving, mining and monitoring.
  • Must be scalable, robust, polite and extensible.

✅ Benefits

  • Makes the content of the web searchable.
  • Can collect data for analysis and protection.
  • Automates work no human could do at this scale.

⚠️ Problems

  • The web is huge and changes all the time.
  • Misbehaving crawlers can harm websites.
  • Bad or malicious pages can trap the crawler.

Original notes from the repository

Source: liquidslr/system-design-notes · Introduction

A web crawler, also known as a spider or robot, is used to discover and collect web content, such as web pages, images, and videos. This chapter focuses on designing a scalable web crawler for search engine indexing.

Applications of Web Crawlers

  1. Search Engine Indexing: Collect web pages to create searchable indexes (e.g., Googlebot).
  2. Web Archiving: Preserve web data for future use (e.g., US Library of Congress).
  3. Web Mining: Extract knowledge from web data (e.g., financial analysis of shareholder reports).
  4. Web Monitoring: Detect copyright or trademark infringements.

Design Challenges

A good web crawler must address:

  • Scalability: Handle billions of pages using parallelization.
  • Robustness: Manage bad HTML, crashes, and malicious links.
  • Politeness: Avoid overwhelming servers with too many requests.
  • Extensibility: Support new content types with minimal changes.

Interview questions and answers

What is a web crawler and what is it used for?
A program that discovers and collects web content by following links. It is used for search indexing, web archiving, web mining and web monitoring.
What are the main design challenges?
Scalability, robustness, politeness and extensibility.
Cross question: Why is politeness a design problem and not just good manners?
A crawler can send thousands of requests per second. If many go to one site, it can overload that site, get the crawler blocked or even count as an attack. The design must limit requests per host.
Cross question: What does extensibility mean for a crawler?
You can add new modules, such as an image downloader or a copyright monitor, without rewriting the core.

📏 Step 1: Requirements and estimation

Hinglish samajh: Requirements: roz nahi, har mahine 1 billion pages crawl karna, sirf HTML, naye aur update hue pages track karna, duplicate content ignore karna, aur 5 saal tak data rakhna. Estimation: 1 billion / 30 din / 86,400 second = lagbhag 400 pages per second, peak 800. Agar ek page 500 KB maana jaye to ek mahine ka 500 TB aur 5 saal ka 30 PB. Isliye distributed storage chahiye aur duplicate detection zaroori hai.

As usual we begin by agreeing on the problem. The crawler must crawl 1 billion web pages per month, collect only HTML content, track new and updated pages, ignore duplicate content and store the crawled data for 5 years. These simple rules already tell us a lot about the size of the system.

Let us do the estimation (chapter 2). 1 billion pages per month is about 1,000,000,000 / 30 / 86,400 = roughly 400 pages per second. Traffic is not flat, so the peak is about twice that: 800 QPS. For storage, assume an average web page is about 500 KB (this is an assumption). Then one month of pages takes 1 billion x 500 KB = 500 TB, and over 5 years (60 months) it is 30 PB (petabytes). That is a very large amount of data, so we need distributed storage and we must avoid storing duplicates.

These numbers decide many things later: 400 pages per second needs many downloader machines working in parallel, and 30 PB means we must be smart about what we store (that is the job of the "Content Seen?" check) and where (disk for most, memory only for popular content).

Requirements

RequirementValue
Crawl rate1 billion pages per month
Content typeHTML only
FreshnessTrack new and updated pages
DuplicatesIgnore duplicate content
RetentionStore for 5 years

Estimation

QuantityCalculationResult
Average QPS1,000,000,000 / 30 days / 86,400 sabout 400 pages per second
Peak QPS2 x 400about 800 pages per second
Storage per month1 billion x 500 KB (assumed page size)500 TB
Storage for 5 years500 TB x 12 x 530 PB

✨ Features

  • 1 billion pages per month, HTML only.
  • Track new and updated pages, skip duplicates.
  • Keep data for 5 years.

✅ Benefits

  • Clear scale numbers to design for.
  • The storage estimate justifies duplicate detection.
  • Peak QPS tells you how many downloaders to plan.

⚠️ Problems

  • Page size is an assumption and may be higher.
  • Some pages are updated often and must be recrawled, which adds load.
  • Compression and deduplication change the final storage size.

  1. Crawl 1 billion web pages per month (400 pages/second, peak 800 QPS).

Interview questions and answers

Estimate the crawl QPS.
1 billion pages a month is about 400 pages per second on average, with a peak of about 800.
Estimate the storage for 5 years.
Assuming 500 KB per page, 1 billion pages is 500 TB per month, so 30 PB over 5 years.
Cross question: How would you reduce the storage?
Detect and skip duplicate content, compress pages, keep only popular content in memory and move old data to cheaper storage.
Cross question: Why only HTML?
It keeps the scope small. The design stays extensible so that other content types can be added later as modules.

🧩 Step 2: High-level design: the components

Hinglish samajh: Crawler ek pipeline hai jisme har component ka ek kaam hai: Seed URLs (shuruaati address), URL Frontier (download ki line), HTML Downloader (page laata hai), DNS Resolver (naam se IP), Content Parser (page theek hai ya nahi), Content Seen? (duplicate content hash se pakadta hai), Content Storage, URL Extractor (links nikalta hai), URL Filter (galat URLs hatata hai), URL Seen? (pehle dekhe URLs) aur URL Storage. Seed URLs ko locality ya topic ke hisaab se chunna achha hota hai.

The crawler is a pipeline of small components, each with one job. Here they are in the order a page flows through them. Seed URLs are the starting points, chosen carefully so that the crawler can reach as many pages as possible. A good approach is to split the space by locality (country) or by topic (sports, healthcare, shopping) and start from several popular sites in each.

The URL Frontier stores the URLs that are waiting to be downloaded, like a to-do list; at its simplest it is a FIFO queue. The HTML Downloader takes URLs from the frontier and downloads the pages, using the DNS Resolver to turn the host name into an IP address. The Content Parser validates the page and discards malformed pages (parsing inside the downloader would slow it down). Content Seen? checks whether we already have this content by comparing hash values, so we do not store the same page twice. Content Storage keeps the HTML pages, mostly on disk with popular content in memory to reduce latency.

Then come the link-handling parts. The URL Extractor pulls out the links from a page (and converts relative links into full addresses). The URL Filter removes unwanted URLs (blacklisted sites, erroneous links, file types we do not want). URL Seen? remembers which URLs have already been visited or are in the frontier, so we do not add them again (a Bloom filter or a hash table works well). URL Storage holds the URLs already visited.

Components and jobs

ComponentJob
Seed URLsStarting points for the crawl
URL FrontierStores URLs waiting to be downloaded (FIFO queue at its simplest)
HTML DownloaderDownloads pages
DNS ResolverConverts a URL host name to an IP address
Content ParserValidates and parses pages, discards malformed ones
Content Seen?Detects duplicate content by comparing hash values
Content StorageStores pages on disk, popular content in memory
URL ExtractorExtracts links from parsed pages
URL FilterExcludes blacklisted or erroneous URLs
URL Seen?Tracks URLs already visited to avoid duplicates
URL StorageStores already visited URLs

✨ Features

  • A pipeline of small, single-purpose components.
  • Duplicate checks for both content and URLs.
  • Seed URLs chosen by locality or topic.

✅ Benefits

  • Each component can be scaled or replaced separately.
  • Duplicate checks save storage and bandwidth.
  • The design is easy to extend.

⚠️ Problems

  • Many components mean many things to run and monitor.
  • The URL-seen check needs a lot of memory at web scale.
  • Poor seed URLs limit what the crawler can discover.

Original notes from the repository

Source: liquidslr/system-design-notes · Components

  1. Seed URLs: Starting points for the crawler.
    • Need to selective as a good starting point that a crawler can utilize to traverse as many links as possible.
    • Can be based on locality based on different popular website or based on topics.
    • Strategies: Categorize by locality or topic (e.g., sports, healthcare).
  2. URL Frontier: Stores URLs to be downloaded.
    • Implemented as a FIFO queue.
  3. HTML Downloader: Downloads web pages from URLs provided by the URL Frontier.
  4. DNS Resolver: Converts URLs to IP addresses.
  5. Content Parser: Validates and parses web pages.
    • Discards malformed pages.
  6. Content Seen?: Checks for duplicate content using hash comparisons (compare the hash values of the two web pages).
  7. Content Storage: Stores HTML pages on disk (popular content in memory to reduce latency).
  8. URL Extractor: Extracts new links from parsed pages.
  9. URL Filter: Excludes blacklisted or erroneous URLs.
  10. URL Seen? Tracks visited URLs to avoid duplication.
  11. URL Storage: Stores already visited URLs.

Interview questions and answers

Name the main components of a web crawler.
Seed URLs, URL frontier, HTML downloader, DNS resolver, content parser, content seen, content storage, URL extractor, URL filter, URL seen and URL storage.
How do you choose seed URLs?
Pick starting points from which the crawler can reach as many pages as possible, for example popular sites divided by country or by topic.
Cross question: Why check content as well as URLs?
Different URLs can lead to the same content (mirrors, copies), so URL checks alone do not prevent duplicate pages from being stored.
Cross question: How do you make the URL seen check memory efficient?
Use a Bloom filter or a compact hash set. A Bloom filter gives a small chance of a false positive but needs far less memory.

🔁 The crawl workflow

Hinglish samajh: Ek crawl cycle: seed URLs frontier mein jaate hain; downloader URL leta hai, DNS se IP nikalkar page download karta hai; parser content check karta hai aur Content Seen? ko deta hai; naya content ho to URL extractor links nikalta hai; links filter hote hain, URL Seen? se duplicate hatate hain aur naye URLs frontier mein jaate hain. Ye loop chalta rehta hai kyunki har naya page naye links dikha sakta hai.

Let us follow one cycle of the crawler from start to finish. Step 1: add the seed URLs to the URL Frontier. Step 2: the HTML Downloader takes a URL from the frontier, finds its IP address with the DNS Resolver, and downloads the page. Step 3: the Content Parser validates the content and passes it to "Content Seen?". Step 4: if the content is new, it is saved and the URL Extractor pulls out all the links. Step 5: the links are filtered and checked against "URL Seen?"; only the new, valid ones are added to the frontier, and the cycle continues.

This loop never ends on its own: every new page can reveal more links. That is why the frontier, the duplicate checks and the filters matter so much; without them the crawler would repeat work forever or wander into useless corners of the web. If the content is a duplicate, the crawler can stop early and skip extracting links from it.

How it works, step by step

  1. Add seed URLs to the URL Frontier.
  2. The HTML Downloader gets URLs from the frontier and fetches the pages, resolving IPs with the DNS Resolver.
  3. The Content Parser validates the page and passes it to Content Seen?.
  4. If the content is new, the URL Extractor pulls out the links.
  5. Links are filtered and checked for duplicates, and the new ones go to the frontier.

✨ Features

  • A continuous loop from frontier to download to links.
  • Duplicate content stops the loop early.
  • Filters keep the loop efficient.

✅ Benefits

  • Easy to explain on a whiteboard.
  • Each step is a separate component that scales on its own.
  • New pages are found automatically.

⚠️ Problems

  • The loop can run forever on huge or infinite sites.
  • Without politeness rules it can overload sites.
  • Failures in one step must not stop the others.

Original notes from the repository

Source: liquidslr/system-design-notes · Workflow

  1. Add Seed URLs to the URL Frontier.
  2. HTML Downloader fetches URLs and resolves their IPs via the DNS Resolver.
  3. Content Parser validates and passes content to the "Content Seen?" component.
  4. If the content is new, extract links via the URL Extractor.
  5. Filter and add unique links to the URL Frontier.

Interview questions and answers

Describe the crawl workflow.
Seeds go into the frontier; the downloader fetches pages; the parser validates them; if the content is new, links are extracted, filtered and the new ones are added to the frontier.
What happens when the content is a duplicate?
The page is not stored again and its links are usually not processed again.
Cross question: When does the crawl end?
In practice it never fully ends, because the web changes all the time. You stop at a configured limit or recrawl pages by freshness rules.
Cross question: Where can this loop be parallelized?
At the downloader (many workers) and at link processing, with the frontier as the shared queue.

🌲 Deep dive: BFS or DFS for walking the web

Hinglish samajh: Web ko ek directed graph samjho: pages nodes hain aur links edges. Crawling ke liye DFS ya BFS ho sakta hai. DFS mein web ki gehrai bahut zyada ho sakti hai aur crawler ek lambi chain mein fans sakta hai, isliye aam taur par BFS (FIFO queue ke saath) use hota hai. Par seedha BFS URL ki priority nahi dekhta aur ek hi host par lagaatar requests bhej sakta hai. URL Frontier in dono samasyaon ko theek karta hai.

The web can be seen as a directed graph: web pages are nodes and hyperlinks (URLs) are edges. Crawling means walking through this graph. There are two classic ways: DFS (depth-first search), which follows one link deeper and deeper before coming back, and BFS (breadth-first search), which visits all links of the current level before going deeper.

DFS is usually a poor choice because the depth of the web can be extremely large. The crawler could dive down one long chain of pages and never get back to the rest. So crawlers normally use BFS, implemented with a FIFO queue: take a URL from the front, add the new links to the back.

But plain BFS has two problems. It does not consider the priority of a URL: a page from a major news site and a page from a spam site are treated the same, though they are not equally important. And it can send many requests to the same host in a row, because pages on the same site link to each other. The URL Frontier (next lesson) fixes both: it adds priority and politeness on top of BFS.

BFS and DFS for crawling

PointDFS (depth-first)BFS (breadth-first)
OrderFollows one chain deep before backing upVisits all links of a level before going deeper
RiskMay get lost in a very deep chain of pagesLarge queue, ignores URL importance
Data structureStackFIFO queue
Usually chosen for crawling?NoYes, improved with priority and politeness

✨ Features

  • The web is a directed graph of pages and links.
  • BFS with a FIFO queue is the usual choice.
  • Plain BFS lacks priority and politeness.

✅ Benefits

  • BFS spreads the crawl wide and avoids dead-end chains.
  • Simple to implement.
  • A solid base on which to add priority and politeness.

⚠️ Problems

  • Plain BFS treats all URLs as equally important.
  • It can hammer one host with consecutive requests.
  • The frontier queue can become very large.

Original notes from the repository

Source: liquidslr/system-design-notes · DFS/BFS

  • The web can be though of as a directed graph where web pages are nodes and hyperlinks (URLs) as edges.
  • BFS is usually used for graph traversal as the depth can be be very deep thus DFS is not ideal.
  • Standard BFS does not take the priority of a URL into consideration, not every page has the same level of quality and importance.

Interview questions and answers

Should a crawler use DFS or BFS?
BFS, because the web is very deep and DFS could get stuck in a long chain. BFS with a FIFO queue spreads out evenly.
What are the limits of standard BFS?
It does not consider URL priority (pages differ in quality) and it can send many requests to the same host in a short time.
Cross question: How would you improve it?
Use a URL frontier with priority queues (important pages first) and per-host queues with delays (politeness).
Cross question: Can you use DFS at all?
Only with a depth limit, for special cases like crawling a single site with a known small depth.

📥 Deep dive: the URL Frontier (politeness, priority, freshness)

Hinglish samajh: URL Frontier crawler ka dil hai. Politeness: ek host se ek samay mein ek hi download aur do downloads ke beech delay; iske liye host ke hisaab se alag FIFO queues aur har queue ke liye ek worker. Priority: zaroori pages (PageRank ya update frequency se) pehle crawl hon; front queues priority sambhalti hain aur back queues politeness. Freshness: pages ko update history aur importance ke hisaab se dobara crawl karo.

The URL Frontier is the heart of a good crawler. It does three jobs: it keeps the crawler polite, it crawls important pages first, and it keeps the content fresh.

Politeness. A crawler should not send too many requests to the same website, because that can overload it. The rule is: download only one page at a time from a host, with a delay between two downloads. To do this, the frontier keeps a mapping from host names to queues, and each worker thread downloads only from its own FIFO queue. The parts are: the queue router (puts each URL into the queue of its host, so that every queue holds URLs of one host only), the mapping table (host to queue), the FIFO queues b1 to bn, the queue selector (connects each worker thread to a queue) and the worker threads 1 to N (download pages one by one from the same host, with a delay).

Priority. Pages differ in value, so the frontier should crawl important URLs earlier; importance can come from PageRank, traffic or how often the page is updated. A prioritizer computes a priority for each URL. There are several queues f1 to fn, each with a priority, and the queue selector picks a queue at random with a bias towards high-priority queues. The front queues manage prioritization, and the back queues manage politeness. A URL passes through the front queues first and then the back queues.

Freshness. Web pages change, so the crawler must recrawl them from time to time. Two strategies help: recrawl based on the update history of the page, and prioritize the recrawl of important pages more often. Also, the frontier can be huge (hundreds of millions of URLs), so we keep the bulk on disk and keep only a buffer in memory with a periodic flush.

What each frontier part does

PartLayerResponsibility
PrioritizerFrontComputes the priority of each URL
Front queues f1 to fnFrontHold URLs by priority; high priority queues are chosen with higher probability
Queue routerBackEnsures each back queue holds URLs of one host only
Mapping tableBackMaps each host to a queue
Back queues b1 to bnBackFIFO queues, one per host (politeness)
Queue selectorBackConnects each worker thread to a queue
Worker threads 1 to NBackDownload pages sequentially from one host with a delay

✨ Features

  • Politeness: one request per host at a time, with a delay.
  • Priority: important URLs first, using front queues.
  • Freshness: recrawl using update history and importance.

✅ Benefits

  • Websites are not overloaded.
  • The best pages are crawled first.
  • The index stays reasonably up to date.

⚠️ Problems

  • Two layers of queues are more complex.
  • The frontier may hold hundreds of millions of URLs, so memory and disk need care.
  • Computing priority (for example PageRank) is itself expensive.

Original notes from the repository

Source: liquidslr/system-design-notes · URL Frontier

  • Politeness:
    • Ensure only one request per host at a time. Add a dealy b/w two download tasks.
    • Use a mapping from hostnames to queues and worker (download) threads.
    • Each downloader thread has a separate FIFO queue and only downloads URLs from that queue.
  • Queue router: Ensures that each queue (b1, b2, … bn) only contains URLs from the same host.
  • Mapping table: It maps each host to a queue.
  • Queue selector: Each worker thread is mapped to a FIFO queue, and it only downloads URLs from that queue. The queue selection logic is done by the Queue selector.
  • Worker thread 1 to N. A worker thread downloads web pages sequentially from the same host. A delay can be added between two download tasks.
  • Priority:
    • Assign higher priority to important pages (e.g., by PageRank or update frequency).
  • Prioritizer: It takes URLs as input and computes the priorities.
  • Queue f1 to fn: Each queue has an assigned priority. Queues with high priority are selected with higher probability.
  • Queue selector: Randomly choose a queue with a bias towards queues with higher priority.
  • Front queues: manage prioritization
  • Back queues: manage politeness
  • Freshness: Recrawl based on update history or importance.

Interview questions and answers

How do you make a crawler polite?
Keep one queue per host and let a single worker download from it, with a delay between requests. A router makes sure each queue holds only one host.
How do you prioritize URLs?
A prioritizer scores each URL (for example by PageRank or update frequency) and puts it in a priority queue. A selector picks queues at random with a bias towards high-priority ones.
Cross question: What is the difference between front and back queues?
Front queues handle priority; back queues handle politeness. A URL first gets a priority, then is routed to the queue of its host.
Cross question: How do you keep pages fresh?
Recrawl pages according to their history of changes and give important pages a shorter recrawl interval.
Cross question: How do you store a frontier with hundreds of millions of URLs?
Keep the bulk on disk and hold only buffers of the head and tail of queues in memory, flushing periodically.

📡 Deep dive: the HTML downloader and robots.txt

Hinglish samajh: HTML downloader pages HTTP se laata hai. Kisi site se download karne se pehle uski robots.txt file padhni chahiye, jisme site ka maalik batata hai ki kaun se pages crawl nahi karne. Download tez karne ke chaar tareeke: distributed crawling (kai servers par), DNS cache (baar baar DNS lookup se bachna), alag alag regions mein crawl servers (website ke paas), aur chhota timeout (dheemi servers par na atakna).

The HTML downloader fetches pages over HTTP. Before downloading anything from a website, a good crawler reads that site's robots.txt file. This is a standard text file in which a website owner tells crawlers which pages they may or may not visit. Respecting it is part of being polite and legal. The crawler should cache the robots.txt of each site and refresh it from time to time, so it does not download it again for every page.

Because downloading is the slowest part, the notes give four performance optimizations. Distributed crawling: run the crawl jobs on many servers, each with many threads, and split the URL space among them. DNS cache: DNS lookups can take 10 to 200 milliseconds and are often synchronous, which blocks the crawler; keeping a cache of host name to IP mappings (updated regularly) avoids repeated lookups. Geographic distribution: place crawl servers in different regions, close to the websites they crawl, for faster downloads. Short timeout: some servers respond slowly or not at all; wait only a limited time and move on, so that one bad server does not block the crawler.

A tiny robots.txt example

␀class="nu">0␀
User-agent: *              ␀class="nu">1␀
Disallow: /private/        ␀class="nu">2␀
Disallow: /cart
Allow: /products/          ␀class="nu">3␀
Crawl-delay: class="nu">5             ␀class="nu">4␀

✨ Features

  • Respect robots.txt rules.
  • Distributed crawling, DNS cache, regional servers and short timeouts.
  • Skip slow or unresponsive servers.

✅ Benefits

  • Faster crawling at lower cost.
  • Good relations with website owners.
  • The crawler is not blocked by one slow site.

⚠️ Problems

  • Caching robots.txt can serve outdated rules for a while.
  • A very short timeout can skip pages that are only temporarily slow.
  • Regional servers add cost and complexity.

Original notes from the repository

Source: liquidslr/system-design-notes · HTML Downloader

  • Robots.txt Compliance: Respect rules in robots.txt files.
  • Performance Optimizations:
    1. Distributed crawling using multiple servers.
    2. Use a DNS cache to avoid repeated lookups.
    3. Geographically distribute crawl servers for faster downloads.
    4. Use a short timeout to avoid slow or unresponsive servers.

Interview questions and answers

What is robots.txt and why do crawlers respect it?
It is a file where a site lists the pages crawlers may not visit. Respecting it is part of polite and responsible crawling.
How do you speed up the downloader?
Distribute crawling across servers, cache DNS lookups, place crawlers geographically near the sites, and use short timeouts.
Cross question: Why is DNS a bottleneck?
DNS lookups can take tens or hundreds of milliseconds and often block the thread, so many lookups add up. A DNS cache removes most of them.
Cross question: What if a server never responds?
A timeout makes the downloader give up and move on, so the crawler is never stuck on a single slow server.

🛡️ Deep dive: robustness and extensibility

Hinglish samajh: Crawler mahino chalta hai aur web ganda aur adbhut hota hai, isliye robustness chahiye: consistent hashing (downloader servers par load baantne ke liye), saari exceptions ko sambhalna aur data validation. Extensibility ke liye pipeline mein naye modules plug karte hain, jaise PNG downloader ya copyright monitor, bina core logic badle. Isse naye features jaldi aur surakshit tareeke se jode jaate hain.

A crawler runs for days and months against the wild, messy web, so it must keep going when things go wrong. The notes list three robustness techniques. Consistent hashing distributes the load among the downloader servers, so that servers can be added or removed with little reshuffling (see chapter 5). Error handling: the web is full of surprises, so exceptions must be handled gracefully and must not crash the system. Data validation: validate the content to make sure it is complete and well formed before trusting it. (The notes also mention saving the crawl state and data so that a crashed crawler can continue from where it stopped.)

Extensibility means that the design can grow without being rewritten. The way to do this is with pluggable modules. The main pipeline stays the same, and new modules are added to process other content types or tasks. For example, a PNG downloader module can fetch images, and a web monitor module can watch content for copyright or trademark violations. Each module plugs into the pipeline after the content parser, so new features never touch the core crawling logic.

✨ Features

  • Consistent hashing, error handling and data validation for robustness.
  • Pluggable modules for new content types.
  • The core pipeline is not changed when adding a module.

✅ Benefits

  • The crawler survives failures and bad data.
  • New features are added quickly and safely.
  • Servers can be added without moving much work.

⚠️ Problems

  • Modules add runtime cost to every page.
  • Poor validation can let bad data into storage.
  • Too many modules can make the pipeline hard to understand.

Original notes from the repository

Source: liquidslr/system-design-notes · Robustness + Extensibility

  1. Consistent Hashing: Distribute load among servers effectively.
  2. Error Handling: Prevent system crashes from exceptions.
  3. Data Validation: Ensure content integrity.
  • Add modules for new content types (e.g., PNG downloader, web monitor).
  • Example: Plug in a module to monitor web content for copyright violations.

Interview questions and answers

How do you make a crawler robust?
Use consistent hashing to distribute load, handle all exceptions gracefully, validate data, and save state so the crawl can resume after a crash.
How do you make it extensible?
Design it as a pipeline where new modules (for example an image downloader or a copyright monitor) can be plugged in without changing the core.
Cross question: Why use consistent hashing for downloaders?
When a downloader fails or is added, only a small share of hosts must move to other servers, so the crawl keeps going with little disruption.
Cross question: How would you add a video crawler?
Write a video downloader module that reads the same URLs and content, and plug it into the pipeline after the content parser.

🪤 Avoiding problematic content: duplicates, spider traps and noise

Hinglish samajh: Har page crawl karne layak nahi hota. Duplicate content (kareeb 30% web pages duplicate hote hain) ko content ke hash se pakadte hain. Spider traps aise pages hain jo crawler ko endless loop mein fansa dete hain; URL ki lambai par limit lagana ek simple bachav hai, aur kuch traps ko haath se blacklist karna padta hai. Data noise (vigyapan, spam, code snippets) ko filter karke hata dena chahiye.

Not every page on the web is worth crawling. Three kinds of problem content need special care. Duplicate content: nearly 30% of web pages are duplicates of other pages. Detect them by comparing hash values (checksums) of the content, which is much faster than comparing text. If the hash is already in the store, the page is a duplicate and is skipped.

Spider traps are pages that make the crawler loop forever. A classic example is an infinitely deep chain of links like www.spidertrapexample.com/foo/bar/foo/bar/foo/bar/..., either by mistake or on purpose. You cannot completely avoid traps automatically, but a simple defense is to limit the maximum URL length. For trickier cases, humans can manually identify the trap and add the site to a blacklist or custom filter.

Data noise is content with little or no value: advertisements, code snippets, spam URLs and similar. This content should be excluded if possible, so the crawler spends its time and storage on useful pages. Together these three protections keep both the storage (30 PB is already huge) and the crawl time under control.

Three kinds of problem content

ProblemWhat it isDefense
Duplicate contentPages that repeat other pages (a large share of the web)Compare content hashes
Spider trapEndless chains of links that trap the crawlerLimit URL length; blacklist known traps
Data noiseAds, spam and other low-value contentFilter it out

✨ Features

  • Hash comparison finds duplicate pages.
  • URL length limits defend against spider traps.
  • Filters remove ads and spam.

✅ Benefits

  • Less storage and bandwidth used.
  • The crawler does not get stuck.
  • The collected data is more useful.

⚠️ Problems

  • Hash comparison finds exact duplicates but misses near-duplicates.
  • A URL length limit may skip some legitimate long URLs.
  • Deciding what is "noise" is subjective.

Original notes from the repository

Source: liquidslr/system-design-notes · Avoiding Problematic Content

  1. Duplicate Content: Detect using hash comparisons.
  2. Spider Traps: Avoid infinite loops with techniques like URL length limits.
  3. Data Noise: Filter irrelevant content like ads or spam.

Interview questions and answers

How do you detect duplicate content?
Compare hash values of the page content. If the hash already exists, the content is a duplicate.
What is a spider trap and how do you handle it?
A trap is an endless chain of links that keeps the crawler busy. Limit the URL length, and blacklist known traps manually.
Cross question: How would you find near-duplicate pages?
Use similarity fingerprints such as shingling or SimHash instead of exact hashes, so pages that differ only slightly are treated as the same.
Cross question: What is data noise?
Content that has no value for the purpose, such as ads, spam pages and code snippets. It should be filtered out.

🏁 Step 4: Wrap up and additional considerations

Hinglish samajh: Summary: web crawler ko scalability, robustness, politeness aur extensibility mein santulan rakhna hota hai. Politeness se websites par load nahi padta aur priority se zaroori pages pehle aate hain. Extra baatein: server-side rendering (JavaScript se bane links ke liye), anti-spam, database replication aur sharding, stateless servers se horizontal scaling, aur analytics.

To close the design, we recall the key lessons. A web crawler has to balance scalability, robustness, politeness and extensibility. Politeness stops us from overloading websites, while priority makes sure that important pages are crawled first. Efficient storage and error handling are essential at this scale.

The notes list extra topics you can raise if time remains. Server-side rendering: many sites generate links dynamically with JavaScript or AJAX, so a plain downloader would miss them; render the page on the server side before parsing. Anti-spam: exclude low-quality and spam pages. Database replication and sharding: scale the data layer. Horizontal scaling: for hundreds or thousands of servers, keep the servers stateless so you can add crawl capacity easily. Availability, consistency and reliability: these concepts are the core of any large system. Analytics: collecting and analyzing data helps fine-tune the system.

✨ Features

  • Balance scalability, robustness, politeness and extensibility.
  • Politeness and priority work together.
  • Extra topics: rendering, anti-spam, sharding, scaling, analytics.

✅ Benefits

  • Gives the interviewer easy follow-up topics.

⚠️ Problems

  • Server-side rendering is expensive.
  • Spam detection is a never-ending contest.
  • Real crawlers need constant tuning.

Key Takeaways

  1. Web crawlers must balance scalability, robustness, politeness, and extensibility.
  2. Politeness prevents overloading servers, while priority ensures important pages are crawled first.
  3. Efficient storage and error handling are crucial for handling large-scale crawling.

Additional Considerations

  • Server-Side Rendering: Handle dynamic content generated by JavaScript or AJAX.
  • Anti-Spam Measures: Exclude low-quality or irrelevant pages.
  • Database Sharding: Scale the data layer using replication and sharding.
  • Horizontal Scaling: Use stateless servers to scale crawl jobs efficiently.
  • Analytics: Collect and analyze data for insights.

Interview questions and answers

Summarize the crawler design in one minute.
Seeds go into a URL frontier that gives priority and politeness; distributed downloaders fetch pages (respecting robots.txt, with DNS caching); parsed content is checked for duplicates; new links are extracted, filtered and checked before returning to the frontier; content is stored on disk with popular data in memory.
What extra things would you mention?
Server-side rendering for JavaScript sites, spam filtering, sharding and replication, horizontal scaling with stateless servers, and analytics.
Cross question: How would you crawl a site built entirely with JavaScript?
Render the page in a headless browser on the server side before parsing, accepting the extra cost for those pages.
Cross question: What would you monitor?
Pages per second, error and timeout rates, queue sizes, duplicate rate, storage growth and per-host request rates.
